title: Limits and continuity
subtitle: How can nearby values determine a reliable conclusion at a point where a formula fails?
prerequisites: Functions, domains, intervals, and absolute value from chapter 1.
Factoring, rational expressions, and radians from chapter 2.
For the lab only: JavaScript functions, loops, and floating-point numbers from chapter 3.
objectives: Distinguish a function value from one-sided and two-sided limits.
Evaluate limits using laws, algebra, and the squeeze theorem with their hypotheses.
Prove linear and nonlinear finite limits from the epsilon–delta definition by choosing a positive radius that works for every eligible nearby input.
Classify discontinuities and asymptotes and apply the intermediate value theorem.

sections.title: 1. Approaching a point without arriving
paragraphs: Suppose a sensor formula gives $f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$. At $x=1$ the denominator is zero, so the formula does not define a value. Nevertheless, at every other input it equals $x+1$. Inputs $0.9$ and $1.1$ give outputs $1.9$ and $2.1$; inputs $0.999$ and $1.001$ give $1.999$ and $2.001$. The nearby outputs suggest $2$. A limit describes this nearby behavior, independently of whether the function has a value at the target input.

We write $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ when values of $f(x)$ become arbitrarily close to $L$ whenever domain inputs $x$ are sufficiently close to $a$ but different from $a$. Throughout, an approach point must have domain inputs arbitrarily near it. Otherwise there is no meaningful approach to inspect. A limit is not a story about an input moving in time: it is a statement about every eligible input in a sufficiently small neighborhood. For the two-sided convention used here, domain inputs must approach $a$ from both sides before comparing left and right limits. For example, $\sqrt{x}$ at $a=0$ has a right-hand approach but no domain inputs approaching from the left.

A left-hand limit, written $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$, restricts inputs to $x<a$. A right-hand limit, written $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$, restricts inputs to $x>a$. When the domain has nearby points on both sides, a finite two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree. For the step function $j(x)=0$ when $x<0$ and $j(x)=1$ when $x\ge0$, $\lim_{x\to0^-}j(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}j(x)=1$. Its two-sided limit does not exist, even though $j(0)$ is defined.

Domain restrictions matter. The function $\sqrt{x}$ has only a right-hand approach at the endpoint zero of its domain $[0,\infty)$. We describe its endpoint behavior by $\lim_{x\to0^+}\sqrt{x}=0$. When discussing continuity on a closed interval, endpoint limits will always be taken from within the interval. Unless physical units are specified, the examples in this chapter use dimensionless inputs and outputs.

Changing the value at the target point never changes a limit. Define $g(x)=x+1$ for $x\ne1$, but set $g(1)$ equal to any number, or leave it undefined. All punctured-neighborhood values are identical, so $\lim_{x\to1}g(x)=2$ in every version. Continuity asks the additional question whether the assigned value is also two. This separation matters when measured data contain a bad reading at one instant: a limiting trend may survive a single corrupted sample, while the record as a function is not continuous at that point. A limit concerns arbitrarily near inputs, not the isolated central value.

The requirement that eligible domain points approach the target avoids vacuous claims. If a function is defined only at the integers, there are no distinct domain points arbitrarily close to the integer $3$. Standard calculus therefore does not assign an ordinary limit there from this domain. In contrast, the domain $(0,\infty)$ has points arbitrarily close to zero from the right, and a right-hand limit at zero is meaningful even though the function may be undefined at zero. At each endpoint or gap, state which approaches the domain actually supports.

There is a useful sequential test in the real line. If $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$, then every sequence of allowed inputs $x_n\ne a$ with $x_n\to a$ has $f(x_n)\to L$. Conversely, if a finite limit fails, some fixed output tolerance is violated arbitrarily close to $a$; choose one violating input within $1/n$ for each $n$ to build a counterexample sequence. Thus two sequences with different output limits disprove a proposed limit. A single favorable sequence cannot prove one, because the definition must cover all nearby inputs.
sections.formula: Two-sided finite limit L ⇔ left-hand limit = L and right-hand limit = L (with both approaches available).
sections.formulaTex: \substack{a\text{ is approached by domain points}\\\text{from both sides}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\iff\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L\right)

sections.title: 2. Laws, cancellation, and squeezing
paragraphs: Limit laws let us assemble complicated conclusions from simpler ones. If $f(x)\to L$ and $g(x)\to M$ as $x\to a$, where $L$ and $M$ are finite real numbers, then $f+g\to L+M$, $f-g\to L-M$, $cf\to cL$ for a fixed constant $c$, and $fg\to LM$. The quotient tends to $L/M$ provided $M\ne0$. Polynomial limits can therefore be found by substitution; rational functions also permit substitution wherever their denominator is nonzero.

A quotient producing $0/0$ after substitution has not evaluated to zero, infinity, or any other answer. The quotient law simply does not apply. Different expressions with this same preliminary form have different limits: $x/x\to1$, $x^2/x\to0$, and $x/x^2$ has no finite two-sided limit as $x\to0$. Algebra can reveal the nearby behavior. Factoring $(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ gives $x+1$ for $x\ne1$, which is exactly the set of inputs relevant to the limit. Cancellation changes the domain if treated as a global identity, but preserves the limit at the hole.

The squeeze theorem handles functions whose values are difficult to track individually. Suppose $p(x)\le f(x)\le q(x)$ for all eligible $x$ sufficiently near $a$, with $x\ne a$. If both $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ tend to the same finite number $L$, then $f(x)$ also tends to $L$. Indeed, once both bounds lie within any prescribed tolerance of $L$, the trapped value must lie there too. The inequalities must hold throughout a neighborhood, not merely at selected sample points.

For $x\ne0$, the bound $-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1$ implies $-x^2\le x^2\sin(1/x)\le x^2$. Both outer functions tend to zero, so the middle function tends to zero despite oscillating more rapidly near zero. Trigonometric arguments here are dimensionless and measured in radians. The oscillation $\sin(1/x)$ alone has no limit: inputs $1/(\pi/2+2\pi n)$ give value $1$, whereas inputs $1/(3\pi/2+2\pi n)$ give $-1$ as the positive integers $n$ grow. Shrinking amplitude, rather than shrinking oscillation frequency, makes the product converge.

Rationalization is another way to uncover a hidden limit. For $x\ne0$ near zero, $(\sqrt{1+x}-1)/x$ becomes $1/(\sqrt{1+x}+1)$ after multiplying by the conjugate. The new expression tends to $1/2$ as $x\to0$. We did not assert that the two formulas agree at zero; they agree on the punctured neighborhood relevant to the limit. Always check the square-root domain $1+x\ge0$ and that the conjugate denominator is nonzero nearby. The same reasoning later becomes the derivative calculation for a square root.

A vanishing factor times a bounded factor tends to zero, even if the bounded factor has no limit. In symbols, if $u(x)\to0$ and $|v(x)|\le C$ near the target, then $|u(x)v(x)|\le C|u(x)|\to0$. Boundedness is essential: $x(1/x)=1$ for $x\ne0$, so a zero-tending factor times an unbounded one need not tend to zero. Nor does the written form $0\cdot\infty$ identify a limit; $x^2(1/x)\to0$ while $x(1/x^2)$ has no finite two-sided limit. Rewrite the actual function and check hypotheses.

Limit laws are local. They require functions to be defined on a common punctured neighborhood of the approach point, and the quotient law requires a nonzero denominator limit. If $g(x)\to M\ne0$, then $g(x)$ is nonzero for every sufficiently near eligible input: require $|g(x)-M|<|M|/2$. This establishes a neighborhood where division is legal. If the denominator limit is zero, further algebra, one-sided analysis, or an unbounded-limit argument is needed. A symbolic substitution that produces $0/0$ is a request for analysis, not a result.
sections.formula: p(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ q(x), p(x) → L, q(x) → L ⇒ f(x) → L.

theorems.title: Why the ordinary limit laws work
theorems.statement: If $f(x)\to L$ and $g(x)\to M$ as $x\to a$ within a common domain, then $f+g\to L+M$ and $fg\to LM$. If $M\ne0$, $f/g\to L/M$ wherever the quotient is defined near $a$.
proof: For the sum, let $\varepsilon>0$. The two limit definitions provide neighborhoods where $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon/2$ and $|g(x)-M|<\varepsilon/2$. In their intersection, the triangle inequality gives $|(f+g)-(L+M)|\le|f-L|+|g-M|<\varepsilon$. The same $x$ must satisfy both estimates; using the smaller of the two $\delta$ values achieves that. This is why a finite number of limits may be combined without changing the order of the quantifiers.

For the product, first use $g\to M$ to make $|g(x)|\le|M|+1$ on a punctured neighborhood. The identity $fg-LM=(f-L)g+L(g-M)$ then gives $|fg-LM|\le(|M|+1)|f-L|+|L||g-M|$. Make the two terms smaller than $\varepsilon/2$ by choosing sufficiently small neighborhoods. Local boundedness is the missing step in the casual statement that a small factor times “something” is small. We did not assume $f$ or $g$ is globally bounded.

For the quotient, $M\ne0$ lets us require $|g(x)-M|<|M|/2$; then $|g(x)|>|M|/2$, so division is defined nearby. Moreover $|1/g-1/M|=|g-M|/(|gM|)\le2|g-M|/|M|^2$, proving reciprocal convergence. Apply the product result to $f$ and $1/g$. If $M=0$, this protection disappears: $1/x$ near zero is an immediate counterexample. The limit laws are proofs about neighborhoods, not formal instructions to substitute a value into an undefined expression.

sections.formulaTex: p(x)\le f(x)\le q(x),\quad p(x),q(x)\to L\implies f(x)\to L

sections.title: 3. Turning closeness into a proof
paragraphs: Graphs and tables help us propose a limit, but every finite display leaves unexamined inputs. The epsilon–delta definition expresses the guarantee a proof must supply. For every $\varepsilon>0$, there must be a $\delta>0$ such that every domain input satisfying $0<|x-a|<\delta$ also satisfies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. Epsilon is the requested output tolerance; delta is an input tolerance sufficient to meet it. The strict inequality $0<|x-a|$ deliberately excludes the point $a$.

The order of choices is essential. A challenger may request any positive $\varepsilon$. We then choose $\delta$, possibly depending on $\varepsilon$, but before knowing which eligible $x$ will be tested. One lucky input is insufficient, and one fixed small tolerance does not establish the limit. If $x$ has units of seconds and $f(x)$ has units of metres, $\delta$ is measured in seconds and $\varepsilon$ in metres; the conversion between them reflects the function’s sensitivity.

For $f(x)=3x-2$ at $a=4$, the proposed limit is $10$. Calculate the exact output error: $|(3x-2)-10|=3|x-4|$. To make this less than $\varepsilon$, it is enough to require $|x-4|<\varepsilon/3$. Proof: given any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/3$. If $0<|x-4|<\delta$, then $|f(x)-10|=3|x-4|<3\delta=\varepsilon$. This completes a proof for all positive tolerances, rather than a numerical check of a few cases.

A smaller positive delta would also work; there is usually no need to find the largest one. For a general nonconstant linear function $mx+b$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/|m|$ to prove its limit at any $a$ is $ma+b$. If $m=0$, the output error is already zero, so any positive $\delta$ works. This separate constant case prevents an invalid division by zero. Nonlinear proofs often require first restricting $|x-a|<1$ to control an extra factor; chapter 5 will use this kind of control when defining derivatives.

A nonlinear epsilon–delta proof often begins by restricting the neighborhood before choosing the final tolerance. To show $1/x\to1$ at $x=1$, first require $|x-1|<1/2$; then $x>1/2$ and $|1/x-1|=|x-1|/|x|\le2|x-1|$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1/2,\varepsilon/2)$. Every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-1|<\delta$ satisfies both the denominator bound and the requested output bound. This proof avoids trying to choose a $\delta$ that depends on the unknown test input.

To disprove a proposed finite limit $L$, it is enough to find one positive $\varepsilon_0$ such that every proposed $\delta>0$ admits an eligible $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ but $|f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon_0$. For example, the right and left values of the step function near zero stay one unit apart. No single number can be within less than half a unit of both branches. Another route is to produce two approach sequences with different output limits. These are constructive failures of the universal claim, not merely statements that a graph looks jumpy.

Proofs should state the candidate limit before searching for delta. Algebra then expresses the output error in terms of the input distance. For a polynomial one often factors a difference; for a reciprocal one first bounds the denominator away from zero; for an oscillating function one bounds its amplitude. The final sentence must use the chosen delta for an arbitrary eligible input. A table of ten increasingly close inputs can help guess $L$ or detect an algebra mistake, but no finite table supplies the required universal guarantee.

The order of the quantifiers is the heart of a limit proof. In $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$, an arbitrary positive output tolerance $\varepsilon$ is announced first. We must then choose an input tolerance $\delta>0$ that works for every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$. A choice of $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, on fixed constants in the function, and on the fixed point $a$; it cannot depend on the particular $x$ that arrives afterward. This explains why checking a long table of inputs is only evidence. The table picks finitely many $x$ values, while the proof must handle all sufficiently close inputs at once. It also explains why the value $f(a)$ is irrelevant to the limit: the punctured condition deliberately excludes $x=a$. When a bound contains a factor such as $|x+a|$, first keep $x$ in a simple neighborhood of $a$ so that factor has a uniform bound, and only then choose $\delta$ to control $\varepsilon$.

For $f(x)=1/x$ on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ near $2$, the output error is $|1/x-1/2|=|x-2|/(2|x|)$. The denominator moves with $x$, so first require $|x-2|<1$. Every input in that band has $x>1$, giving the uniform bound $1/(2|x|)<1/2$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1,2\varepsilon)$ before an input is named. Then every eligible $x$ with $0<|x-2|<\delta$ has output error $<|x-2|/2<\delta/2\le\varepsilon$. Problem 04.38 asks you to build this proof and compare the sufficient radius with the greatest one. Figure 4.4 gives a separate $x^2$ view of how the output request and input choice interact.

The order is $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(f)$, followed by the punctured-input implication. If we choose $\delta$ after seeing each $x$, we can make the antecedent false and claim success without controlling any output. Problem 04.39 exposes that trap for $1/x$ near zero. One failed proposed radius at a tolerance rejects that radius only; a failed limit needs one fixed positive output tolerance that defeats every positive radius. Keep those claims distinct when you write a counterexample.
sections.formula: For every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0: 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.

sections.title: 4. Unbounded behavior and distant behavior
paragraphs: An infinite limit describes unbounded growth, not convergence to a real number called infinity. The notation $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=+\infty$ means that for every threshold $M>0$, some $\delta>0$ makes $f(x)>M$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$ within the domain. For $-\infty$, require $f(x)<-M$ instead. One-sided versions restrict $x$ to the indicated side. These statements demand arbitrarily large magnitude, not merely an impressive value on a screen.

For $1/x^2$ as $x\to0$, choose $\delta=1/\sqrt M$. Then $0<|x|<\delta$ implies $1/x^2>M$, proving the limit is $+\infty$. By contrast, $\lim_{x\to0^-}1/x=-\infty$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}1/x=+\infty$. Its two-sided limit is neither $+\infty$ nor $-\infty$. A vertical line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote when at least one one-sided limit there is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. A missing value alone does not create an asymptote: the hole in $(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ has finite nearby behavior.

Limits at infinity ask a different question: what happens when inputs grow without bound? The statement $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to+\infty$ means that every $\varepsilon>0$ admits a threshold $R$ such that $x>R$ in the domain implies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. If such a finite limit exists, $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote in that direction. Dividing numerator and denominator by $x$ shows $(2x+1)/(x-3)=(2+1/x)/(1-3/x)\to2$ as $x\to+\infty$, and also as $x\to-\infty$. Its denominator forbids $x=3$. A horizontal asymptote describes distant behavior; it does not forbid the graph from crossing that line elsewhere.

At a vertical pole, orientation matters. Near $x=3$, the function $1/(x-3)$ has $\lim_{x\to3^-}1/(x-3)=-\infty$ and $\lim_{x\to3^+}1/(x-3)=+\infty$. Its magnitude becomes arbitrarily large, but there is no two-sided $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ limit. For $1/(x-3)^2$, both one-sided values tend to $+\infty$. The parity of the denominator power explains this sign difference. A rational function can also have a removable zero-over-zero hole rather than a pole, so factor before classifying a suspicious denominator zero.

For rational functions at infinity, divide numerator and denominator by the highest denominator power or compare leading degrees. If the numerator degree is smaller, the limit is zero; if equal, the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients. If the numerator degree is larger, there is no finite horizontal limit, though polynomial division may reveal a slant or curved asymptote. Sign and direction still matter: $\sqrt{x^2+1}/x\to1$ as $x\to+\infty$ but $\sqrt{x^2+1}/x\to-1$ as $x\to-\infty$, because $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$, not $x$ on the negative half-line.

Being unbounded is weaker than tending to infinity. For $x>0$, the function $g(x)=x(1+\sin x)$ grows arbitrarily large along $x=\pi/2+2\pi n$ for nonnegative integers $n$, where $g(x)=2x$. Yet it returns to zero along $x=3\pi/2+2\pi n$. Both sequences of inputs tend to $+\infty$, so no single threshold can force $g(x)>M$ for every later input, even when $M=1$. Nor does $g(x)$ approach a finite horizontal limit. This pair of sequences is a practical way to disprove a proposed distant limit: find two arbitrarily distant input families with incompatible output behavior. The function is continuous throughout its domain, so continuity alone cannot guarantee a limit at infinity.

The threshold definition keeps infinity honest. To prove $1/x^2\to+\infty$ as $x\to0$, a requested height $M>0$ is met whenever $0<|x|<1/\sqrt M$. To prove $1/x\to0$ as $x\to+\infty$, a requested tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ is met whenever $x>1/\varepsilon$. These are different quantifier patterns: input distance from a finite point in the first, input size beyond a threshold in the second. Neither proof treats infinity as a real number that can be substituted into an algebraic expression.

sections.title: 5. Continuity and values that cannot be skipped
paragraphs: A function is continuous at an interior point $a$ when $f(a)$ exists, the finite limit as $x\to a$ exists, and that limit equals $f(a)$. Each condition matters. Defining the hole example to have value $7$ at $x=1$ leaves its limit equal to $2$ and creates a removable discontinuity. Redefining just that value to $2$ repairs it. A jump cannot be repaired by choosing a different value at its single break, because the one-sided limits disagree. Infinite discontinuities also cannot be repaired by inserting one finite value.

Polynomials are continuous everywhere, rational functions wherever their denominators do not vanish, and compositions of continuous functions are continuous wherever defined. The composition assertion requires the inner function to approach a point where the outer function is continuous. Continuity on $[a,b]$ means continuity at every interior point, right continuity at $a$, and left continuity at $b$. This convention matches an instrument observed over a finite time interval, where there may be no recorded earlier or later time.

The intermediate value theorem states that if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, with $a<b$, then for every number $N$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, there exists $c\in[a,b]$ with $f(c)=N$. If $N$ lies strictly between the endpoint values, $c\in(a,b)$. The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness or a formula for $c$. A continuous temperature record rising from 18 °C to 23 °C must pass through 20 °C, provided continuity is a justified model assumption; a sensor that rounds to whole degrees reports a different, discontinuous function.

As a mathematical application, $f(x)=x^3+x-1$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, and its endpoint values are $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=1$. Therefore it has a zero strictly between them. Computing $f(0.6)=-0.184$ and $f(0.7)=0.043$ narrows the guaranteed interval to $(0.6,0.7)$. The sign computations become conclusive because continuity supplies the theorem’s hypothesis. A jump from $-1$ to $1$ would have the same endpoint signs without any zero. Chapter 9 turns repeated interval narrowing into a numerical algorithm.

To locate the value rather than trust a drawing, assume first that $f(a)<N<f(b)$. Bisect $[a,b]$ repeatedly, retaining a closed half whose left endpoint has value at most $N$ and whose right endpoint has value at least $N$. If a midpoint already has value $N$, the claim is proved. Otherwise the retained intervals have length $(b-a)/2^n$ after $n$ bisections. The theorem below explains exactly how completeness gives their common point and how continuity forces its value. Finite bisection only brackets that point; it does not prove that the process reaches it in finitely many steps.

Existence is separate from uniqueness. The continuous function $x^3-x$ changes sign from $-6$ at $-2$ to $6$ at $2$, so the theorem guarantees at least one root. In fact it has three: $-1$, $0$, and $1$. Conversely, a function may have a root without a sign change, as $x^2$ does at zero. A sign change is a sufficient certificate for a continuous function, not a necessary condition for every root. Later, monotonicity can certify that a particular bracket contains at most one root.

Continuity is a model assumption when the function represents physical data. A water level can jump in a recorded table because the sensor rounds values or samples discretely, even when the underlying level varies continuously. Conversely, a valve may introduce a real abrupt change in a rate model. Before invoking the intermediate value theorem, identify the function to which it applies: the idealized physical quantity, the rounded readout, or a piecewise rule. Matching endpoint numbers alone cannot replace continuity on the whole closed interval.
sections.formula: Continuity at a: lim as x → a of f(x) = f(a).

theorems.title: Why a continuous function cannot skip an intermediate value
theorems.statement: If $a<b$, $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, and $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then some $c\in[a,b]$ satisfies $f(c)=N$.
proof: If $N$ equals an endpoint value, use that endpoint. Otherwise define $g=f$ when $f(a)<N<f(b)$, and $g=2N-f$ when $f(b)<N<f(a)$. In either case $g$ is continuous, $g(a)<N<g(b)$, and $g(c)=N$ exactly when $f(c)=N$. Set $I_0=[a,b]$. At each step bisect $I_n=[a_n,b_n]$ and retain a half with $g(a_{n+1})\le N\le g(b_{n+1})$. Equality at a midpoint already finishes the proof. The halves are closed and nested, and $b_n-a_n=(b-a)/2^n\to0$.

Completeness of the real numbers means every nonempty set bounded above has a least upper bound. The left endpoints form a nondecreasing set bounded by $b$; let $c=\sup\{a_n:n\ge0\}$. For each fixed $n$, all later left endpoints lie in $[a_n,b_n]$, so $a_n\le c\le b_n$. Thus $c$ lies in every retained interval. Because their widths tend to zero, $0\le c-a_n\le b_n-a_n\to0$ and $0\le b_n-c\le b_n-a_n\to0$: both endpoint sequences approach the same real point. This is the nested-interval step supplied by completeness, not by a finite decimal approximation.

Continuity of $g$ at $c$ along the interval gives $g(a_n)\to g(c)$ and $g(b_n)\to g(c)$, using the appropriate one-sided continuity if $c$ is an endpoint. Since $g(a_n)\le N\le g(b_n)$ at every step, taking these limits gives $g(c)\le N\le g(c)$, hence $g(c)=N$ and therefore $f(c)=N$. For descending original endpoint data, $f(a_n)$ and $f(b_n)$ have the opposite bracket order; the transformed $g$ keeps the ascending one. The proof needs continuity throughout the closed interval; endpoint signs alone would permit a jump that skips $N$.

sections.title: An ε–δ proof with the constants exposed
paragraphs: To prove $\lim_{x\to3}x^2=9$ from the definition, begin with the output error: $|x^2-9|=|x-3||x+3|$. The first factor is controlled directly by the input distance, but the second factor also changes with $x$. A claim such as “take $\delta=\varepsilon/|x+3|$” is not a valid fixed choice, because $\delta$ must be selected before an arbitrary nearby $x$ is given. We need one bound for $|x+3|$ throughout a whole input neighborhood.

First require $|x-3|<1$. Then $2<x<4$, hence $5<x+3<7$. Therefore $|x^2-9|\le7|x-3|$, including at $x=3$. Given any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/7)$. If $0<|x-3|<\delta$, both requirements hold and $|x^2-9|<7\delta\le\varepsilon$. The conclusion follows for every eligible $x$, not merely along sampled values or one side of $3$. The strict inequality remains valid even when $\delta$ equals one of the two bounds. A smaller positive $\delta$ also works; the proof seeks a fixed sufficient choice, not the largest possible one.

The same technique proves continuity of the square function at any real center $a$. If $|x-a|<1$, then $|x+a|=|(x-a)+2a|\le|x-a|+2|a|<1+2|a|$. Thus $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/(1+2|a|))$ works for $|x^2-a^2|<\varepsilon$. The number 1 is a convenient local neighborhood, not a mysterious theorem constant; another fixed positive radius could be used with a corresponding bound.

A numerical plot can suggest that $x^2$ approaches $9$ near $3$, but it cannot express the order of quantifiers: every $\varepsilon$ must have a $\delta$ that works for every $x$ in the punctured neighborhood. Once the estimate is written, the proof is short and also reveals a local sensitivity bound. It does not require evaluating $x^2$ at $x=3$ to establish the limit, although the function value there happens to agree.

The same pattern clarifies units. If $x$ is time and $f(x)$ is position, $\delta$ has time units and $\varepsilon$ has length units; a coefficient such as the local bound on a derivative has units of length per time. Writing $\delta=\varepsilon/7$ without units is meaningful only when the function and variables are dimensionless or the constant 7 carries the corresponding conversion units. The neighborhood radius written as $1$ in $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/7)$ also needs time units in that application. A mathematical proof may suppress units, but an application should not. A valid limit establishes arbitrarily fine local control; it does not claim that a finite-resolution measuring device can verify every tolerance.

A second proof pattern uses the triangle inequality directly. To show $|x|\to|a|$ as $x\to a$, use the reverse triangle inequality $||x|-|a||\le|x-a|$. Given any output tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon$. Every eligible input within that delta has output error below $\varepsilon$. This works at positive, negative, and zero centers without splitting into cases, and it proves continuity of absolute value everywhere. More generally, suppose there are fixed constants $\rho>0$ and $0\le K<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(a)|\le K|x-a|$ for every domain input with $|x-a|<\rho$. Then $f$ has a limit equal to $f(a)$ there: choose $\delta=\min(\rho,\varepsilon/K)$ if $K>0$, or any $0<\delta\le\rho$ if $K=0$. Such a local Lipschitz estimate is stronger than continuity because it gives an explicit linear response bound. The proof still depends on checking the inequality on a whole neighborhood, not merely at one plotted input. For a nonlinear function the best local constant may depend on the chosen neighborhood, which is why the earlier quadratic argument first confined $x$ near its center.

The limit and derivative questions are related but not interchangeable. The absolute-value function approaches zero at zero from both sides and is continuous there, yet its left and right slope limits differ. Conversely, a function can have a limit at a point where its displayed formula is undefined. Keep the output-closeness question separate from the quotient-of-changes question as you move to chapter 5.

When choosing $\delta$, first isolate what depends on the arbitrary nearby input. For a product such as $|x-a||x+a|$, a preliminary restriction $|x-a|<1$ provides a fixed bound on the second factor; only then choose the remaining part of $\delta$ from $\varepsilon$. The chosen $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ and the fixed target $a$, but it may not depend on the particular $x$ selected afterward. To disprove a proposed limit, reverse the task: find one positive $\varepsilon$ for which every positive $\delta$ admits a domain point violating the required bound. Writing these quantifiers in order is more informative than a numerical table.

The local-bound method also works for $x^2$ near $2$: requiring $|x-2|<1$ gives $|x+2|<5$, so $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/5)$ is sufficient. That proof answers whether we can guarantee a requested tolerance. A learner who chooses epsilon and delta independently faces another question: does this particular delta work for every input in its open band? In Figure 4.4, predict the answer before opening the comparison. A point exactly on an input-band boundary is excluded from the test.

A failed choice needs an input strictly inside the band whose output reaches or crosses the requested boundary. Finding one rejects that choice of delta; it does not reject the limit, because a smaller choice may work. After the investigation, derive the greatest valid symmetric radius and test the equality case in Problems 36 and 37.

examples.title: Repairing a hole
examples.problem: For $x\ne2$, let $r(x)=(x^2-4)/(x-2)$. Find its limit at $2$ and choose $r(2)$ to make the function continuous.
steps: Factor $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. For every $x\ne2$, cancellation gives $r(x)=x+2$.
The limit law for sums gives $\lim_{x\to2}(x+2)=4$. This applies from both sides.
Continuity requires the newly assigned value to equal the limit. At $x=1.99$ and $2.01$ the exact outputs are $3.99$ and $4.01$, providing a cross-check.
examples.answer: The limit is $4$, and the unique continuous extension has $r(2)=4$. The original quotient remains undefined at $2$.

examples.title: A tolerance guarantee for a calibration rule
examples.problem: A position model is $s(t)=5t+2$ metres, with $t$ in seconds. Prove its limit at $t=3$ seconds is $17$ metres and guarantee an error below $0.02$ metres.
steps: The slope is $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Thus $|s(t)-17|=5|t-3|$ with the appropriate units.
For any requested $\varepsilon>0$ metres, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/(5\,\mathrm{m/s})$. Every eligible time within $\delta$ of $3$ seconds has position error below $\varepsilon$.
For $\varepsilon=0.02$ metres, take $\delta=0.004$ seconds. The input inequality must be strict to guarantee a strict output error.
examples.answer: The limit is $17\,\mathrm{m}$. Every $t$ satisfying $0<|t-3|<0.004$ seconds produces $|s(t)-17|<0.02$ metres.

examples.title: Two one-sided limits decide a jump
examples.problem: For $f(x)=2+x$ when $x<0$ and $f(x)=3-x$ when $x\ge0$, find its one-sided limits and decide whether changing $f(0)$ can make it continuous.
steps: On the left branch, $2+x$ approaches $2$ as $x\to0$ from negative inputs.
On the right branch, $3-x$ approaches $3$ as $x\to0$ from positive inputs.
The two values differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
Assigning a new value at the single input zero leaves all nearby branch values unchanged.
examples.answer: Left limit $2$, right limit $3$; there is a jump and no choice of $f(0)$ repairs continuity.

examples.title: Rationalization resolves a zero-over-zero form
steps: The square root requires $x\ge-1$; this leaves eligible inputs on both sides of zero.
For $x\ne0$, multiply by the conjugate to obtain $1/[\sqrt{1+x}+1]$.
The denominator approaches $2$ and stays nonzero near zero.
Apply the quotient law to the simplified expression, which agrees with the original where the limit is tested.
examples.answer: The two-sided limit is $1/2$; the original expression remains undefined at $x=0$.

examples.title: Squeezing oscillation without counting waves
examples.problem: Find $\lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos(1/x)$, and explain why sampling is not a proof.
steps: For every nonzero $x$, $-1\le\cos(1/x)\le1$.
Multiplying by $x^2\ge0$ gives $-x^2\le x^2\cos(1/x)\le x^2$.
Both bounding functions approach zero, so the squeeze theorem gives the limit zero.
A finite set of samples cannot inspect all increasingly rapid oscillations.
examples.answer: The limit is zero; the amplitude bound proves it for every sufficiently near input.

examples.title: An epsilon–delta certificate for a reciprocal
steps: First impose $|x-1|<1/2$ so that $x>1/2$ and division remains safe.
For any $\varepsilon>0$ choose $\delta=\min(1/2,\varepsilon/2)$.
If $0<|x-1|<\delta$, the output error is strictly below $\varepsilon$.
examples.answer: The displayed delta works for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every eligible input in its punctured neighborhood.

examples.title: A vertical pole needs two directions
examples.problem: Classify the behavior of $1/(x-3)$ and $1/(x-3)^2$ as $x$ approaches $3$.
steps: For $x<3$, $x-3$ is negative and tends to zero, so its reciprocal tends to $-\infty$.
For $x>3$, the reciprocal tends to $+\infty$.
Squaring the denominator makes both one-sided values positive and arbitrarily large.
Neither function has a finite limit at $3$; only the squared reciprocal has a two-sided $+\infty$ limit.
examples.answer: Both have vertical asymptote $x=3$; the first has opposite one-sided infinite behavior, the second tends to $+\infty$ from both sides.

examples.title: The intermediate value theorem gives a bracket
examples.problem: Show that $f(x)=x^3-2$ has a root in $(1,2)$, then give the first two bisection brackets.
steps: The polynomial is continuous on $[1,2]$, with $f(1)=-1$ and $f(2)=6$.
The intermediate value theorem gives at least one root in $(1,2)$.
At each midpoint, retain the half whose endpoint values have opposite signs. Continuity guarantees that a root remains in that half; this is the bisection invariant.
At midpoint $1.5$, $f=1.375>0$, so retain $[1,1.5]$.
examples.answer: The first two retained brackets are $[1,1.5]$ and $[1.25,1.5]$. Each contains a root; the second has width $0.25$.

misconceptions: “The limit equals the function value.” A limit ignores the target point; a function can have limit 2 there and assigned value 7. Equality is an additional continuity condition.
“A graph that looks connected proves continuity.” Finite resolution can hide holes, jumps, and rapid oscillations. A proof must control every sufficiently nearby input.
“Opposite signs guarantee a root.” They do so under the intermediate value theorem’s continuity hypothesis; a step function can skip zero.

lab.title: Inspect removable and jump discontinuities
lab.description: Compare two dimensionless functions near $x=1$. The removable example equals $x+1$ for $x\ne1$ and takes the code value atPoint at $x=1$; that assigned point is reported in the console rather than plotted. The jump example equals $x+1$ for $x<1$ and adds the code value jump to $x+1$ for $x>1$; no value at $x=1$ is assigned. Separate plots prevent the renderer from drawing a false connection across the break. The console table reports distances $h$ and the four corresponding outputs.
tasks: Before running, predict whether changing atPoint can change either limit. State which value makes the removable example continuous.
Set jump = 0, then jump = -2. Explain which choices of jump give the jump example a two-sided limit at $x=1$, and why.
Reduce radius to 0.01. Why can a narrower graph strengthen a conjecture without proving it? Explain why the two sides were plotted separately.

Within the existing table loop, change k <= 6 to k <= 17. After the const h = 10 ** (-k); line, add const x = 1 + h; and console.log(k, (x*x - 1)/(x - 1), x + 1); on separate lines. Compare the new outputs and explain why rounding and division by zero eventually make the numerical evidence unreliable. Explain why a radius below machine resolution cannot produce distinct one-sided plot points.
lab.expected: At the default radius, four plots each contain 100 finite points strictly on their stated side of $x=1$. A radius too small to move the first samples away from $x=1$ is rejected; sampled values that overflow are also rejected. At $h=0.1$ the table gives $(1.9,2.1,1.9,3.1)$, up to floating-point rounding. At $h=10^{-6}$ it gives $(1.999999,2.000001,1.999999,3.000001)$. The removable limit is exactly $2$ despite $f(1)=7$. The jump limits are exactly $2$ and $3$, so its two-sided limit does not exist. With jump = 0 both jump limits are $2$; with jump = -2 they are $2$ and $0$. After the edit in task 4, the computed input rounds to $x=1$ at $k=16$ and $17$, so the direct quotient prints NaN while x + 1 prints 2.

exercises.question: For $f(x)=(x^2-4)/(x-2)$ with $x\ne2$, find its limit as $x\to2$ and say whether $f$ is continuous there.
exercises.hint: Factor the numerator, but retain the original domain.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne2$, factor and cancel to get $f(x)=x+2$, so $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4$. The original function has no value at $2$, so it is not continuous there. Defining $f(2)=4$ would make a continuous extension.

exercises.question: Let $f(x)=x+1$ for $x<0$ and $f(x)=2-x$ for $x\ge0$. Find both one-sided limits at zero and the two-sided limit.
exercises.hint: Use the appropriate branch on each side.
exercises.solution: For $x<0$, $f(x)=x+1\to1$ as $x\to0^-$. For $x\ge0$, $f(x)=2-x\to2$ as $x\to0^+$. The one-sided limits differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist; $f(0)=2$ agrees only with the right-hand limit.

exercises.question: Use two sequences to show that $\sin(1/x)$ has no limit as $x\to0$.
exercises.hint: Choose inputs whose reciprocals have sine values $1$ and $-1$.
exercises.solution: Let $x_n=1/(\pi/2+2\pi n)$ and $y_n=1/(3\pi/2+2\pi n)$. Both tend to $0$ through positive inputs, but $\sin(1/x_n)=1$ and $\sin(1/y_n)=-1$. A common limit cannot have both values.

exercises.question: Find $\lim_{x\to3}(x^2-9)/(x-3)$. Is the displayed function continuous at 3?
exercises.hint: Factor the numerator, but retain the domain restriction.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne3$, $\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=x+3$, so the limit as $x\to3$ is $6$. The displayed quotient is undefined at $3$ and therefore not continuous there. Assigning the value $6$ gives a continuous extension.

exercises.question: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin(1/x)$, with the function defined only for $x\ne0$.
exercises.hint: Bound the absolute value; multiplying by negative $x$ would reverse an inequality.
exercises.solution: Because $|\sin(1/x)|\le1$, we have $-|x|\le x\sin(1/x)\le|x|$ for $x\ne0$. Both bounds tend to $0$, so the squeeze theorem gives $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin(1/x)=0$. A function value at zero is unnecessary.

exercises.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R$ have points arbitrarily close to $a$ from both sides, and let $f,g:D\to\mathbb R$. If $f(x)\to2$ and $g(x)\to-3$ as $x\to a$ through $D$, prove from the limit definition that $f(x)+g(x)\to-1$.
exercises.hint: Split a requested output tolerance between the two errors.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, the two limit definitions give $\delta_1,\delta_2>0$ such that $|f(x)-2|<\varepsilon/2$ when $x\in D$ and $0<|x-a|<\delta_1$, and $|g(x)+3|<\varepsilon/2$ when $x\in D$ and $0<|x-a|<\delta_2$. Choose $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\delta_2)$. For every $x\in D$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$, $|(f(x)+g(x))-(-1)|\le|f(x)-2|+|g(x)+3|<\varepsilon$.

exercises.question: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x}$.
exercises.hint: Rationalize with $\sqrt{4+x}+2$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne0$ with $x\ge-4$, rationalization gives $\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x}=\frac1{\sqrt{4+x}+2}$. The denominator tends to $4$, so the limit is $1/4$. The original quotient remains undefined at zero.

exercises.question: Prove that $x^2\cos(1/x)$ tends to zero as $x\to0$.
exercises.hint: Use $|\cos(1/x)|\le1$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne0$, $|x^2\cos(1/x)|\le x^2$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choosing $0<|x|<\sqrt\varepsilon$ makes the magnitude smaller than $\varepsilon$. Thus the limit is $0$, despite the oscillating cosine factor.

exercises.question: Why does the rule 'a factor tends to zero, so the product tends to zero' fail for $x(1/x)$ as $x\to0$?
exercises.hint: Check whether the other factor is bounded.
exercises.solution: For every $x\ne0$, $x(1/x)=1$, so its limit is $1$. The factor $1/x$ is unbounded near zero; the bounded-factor argument does not apply. The expression $0\cdot\infty$ does not determine a limit.

exercises.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R$ have points arbitrarily close to $a$ from both sides, and let $f,g:D\to\mathbb R$. If $f(x)\to3$ and $g(x)\to-2$ as $x\to a$ through $D$, find the limit of $\frac{2f(x)-g(x)}{g(x)}$.
exercises.hint: Check the denominator limit before applying quotient laws.
exercises.solution: The numerator tends to $2(3)-(-2)=8$ and the denominator to $-2\ne0$. By quotient laws the limit is $8/(-2)=-4$. The nonzero denominator limit also ensures $g(x)\ne0$ sufficiently near $a$.

exercises.question: Give a complete epsilon–delta proof that $7-2x$ tends to $1$ as $x$ tends to $3$.
exercises.hint: Express the output error as a multiple of $|x-3|$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/2$. For every $x$ with $0<|x-3|<\delta$, $|(7-2x)-1|=2|x-3|<2\delta=\varepsilon$. This proves the limit.

exercises.question: Prove $\lim_{x\to1}\frac1x=1$ with an explicit $\delta(\varepsilon)$.
exercises.hint: Keep $x$ away from zero before bounding $|1/x-1|$.
exercises.solution: Require $|x-1|<1/2$, which gives $x>1/2$ and hence $|1/x-1|=|x-1|/|x|<2|x-1|$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1/2,\varepsilon/2)$. Then $0<|x-1|<\delta$ makes the output error smaller than $\varepsilon$.

exercises.question: Give a complete $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ proof that $5x-1$ tends to $9$ as $x\to2$.
exercises.hint: Express the output error as a multiple of $|x-2|$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/5$. If $0<|x-2|<\delta$, then $|(5x-1)-9|=5|x-2|<5\delta=\varepsilon$. This covers every eligible input.

exercises.question: Prove directly that $1/x$ tends to $1$ as $x\to1$.
exercises.hint: Keep $x$ above $1/2$ before bounding the quotient.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1/2,\varepsilon/2)$. When $0<|x-1|<\delta$, $x>1/2$ and $|1/x-1|=|x-1|/|x|<2|x-1|<\varepsilon$. The fixed denominator bound makes $\delta$ independent of the test input.

exercises.question: Disprove the claim $\lim_{x\to0}x^2=1$ by giving a fixed output tolerance.
exercises.hint: Take $\varepsilon_0=1/2$ and choose a small nonzero $x$ for any proposed $\delta$.
exercises.solution: Fix $\varepsilon_0=1/2$. Given any $\delta>0$, choose $0<x<\min(\delta,1/2)$. Then $x^2<1/4$, so $|x^2-1|>3/4>\varepsilon_0$. No $\delta$ meets the proposed limit; the true limit is $0$.

exercises.question: Find the one-sided limits of $1/(x-2)$ at 2 and identify its vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
exercises.hint: Track the denominator’s sign near 2 and its size far away.
exercises.solution: As $x\to2^-$, $x-2$ is negative and tends to zero, so $1/(x-2)\to-\infty$. From the right it tends to $+\infty$. Thus $x=2$ is a vertical asymptote, with no two-sided infinite limit of one sign. As $x\to\pm\infty$, the quotient tends to $0$, giving horizontal asymptote $y=0$.

exercises.question: Use the threshold definition to prove that $1/x^2$ tends to $+\infty$ as $x\to0$.
exercises.hint: Solve $1/x^2>M$ for $|x|$.
exercises.solution: Given any $M>0$, choose $\delta=1/\sqrt M$. If $0<|x|<\delta$, then $x^2<1/M$ and $1/x^2>M$. This proves $1/x^2\to+\infty$ as $x\to0$ in the threshold sense.

exercises.question: Find the left and right infinite limits of $1/(x-3)$ at $x=3$.
exercises.hint: Track the sign of $x-3$ before taking its reciprocal.
exercises.solution: As $x\to3^-$, $x-3$ is negative and tends to zero, so $1/(x-3)\to-\infty$. From the right, $1/(x-3)\to+\infty$. The two-sided limit does not exist.

exercises.question: Find $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{3x^2+1}{x^2-2}$.
exercises.hint: Divide numerator and denominator by $x^2$.
exercises.solution: Dividing by $x^2$ gives $\frac{3+1/x^2}{1-2/x^2}$. As $x\to+\infty$, the numerator tends to $3$ and the denominator to $1$, so the limit is $3$.

exercises.question: Find both limits of $\frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}}{x}$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$.
exercises.hint: Factor $|x|$ out of the square root.
exercises.solution: The quotient equals $\frac{|x|}{x}\sqrt{1+1/x^2}$. The square-root factor tends to $1$. Since $|x|/x$ is $1$ for positive $x$ and $-1$ for negative $x$, the limits are $1$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $-1$ as $x\to-\infty$.

exercises.question: Does $f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ have a vertical asymptote at $x=1$? State its nearby line.
exercises.hint: Cancel only on the original punctured domain.
exercises.solution: No. For $x\ne1$, $f(x)=x+1\to2$ as $x\to1$, so there is no divergence. The graph lies on $y=x+1$ near $1$, with a removable hole at $(1,2)$.

exercises.question: Let $f(x)=x+2$ for $x<0$ and $f(x)=2-x$ for $x\ge0$. Find both limits at zero and decide continuity.
exercises.hint: Use the branch on each side, then inspect $f(0)$.
exercises.solution: From the left, $x+2\to2$; from the right, $2-x\to2$. Therefore $\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=2$. Since $f(0)=2$, the function is continuous at zero.

exercises.question: Prove that $x^3-2$ has a zero between 1 and 2. Does the intermediate value theorem alone prove it has only one?
exercises.hint: Check continuity and signs before invoking the theorem.
exercises.solution: The polynomial $f(x)=x^3-2$ is continuous on $[1,2]$, and $f(1)=-1<0<f(2)=6$. The intermediate value theorem gives a root in $(1,2)$. That theorem alone does not prove uniqueness; strict increase of $x^3$ supplies a separate uniqueness argument.

exercises.question: Define $f(x)=\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}$ for $x\ne3$. What value at 3 makes $f$ continuous?
exercises.hint: Factor $x^2-9$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne3$, $f(x)=x+3$, so $\lim_{x\to3}f(x)=6$. Defining $f(3)=6$ makes the value match the limit and removes the discontinuity.

exercises.question: Use the intermediate value theorem to show $x^3+x-1$ has a zero in $(0,1)$.
exercises.hint: Check continuity and endpoint signs.
exercises.solution: The polynomial $f(x)=x^3+x-1$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. Since $f(0)=-1<0<f(1)=1$, the intermediate value theorem supplies $c\in(0,1)$ with $c^3+c-1=0$.

exercises.question: Give a continuous function with a sign change across $[-2,2]$ but more than one zero there.
exercises.hint: A factored cubic can have three simple roots.
exercises.solution: Take $f(x)=x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)$. It is continuous, $f(-2)=-6<0<f(2)=6$, and its zeros in $[-2,2]$ are $-1,0,1$. A sign change guarantees existence, not uniqueness.

exercises.question: For $f(x)=x^3-2$ on $[1,2]$, perform two bisection steps and bound the midpoint error after them.
exercises.hint: Evaluate $f(1.5)$ and $f(1.25)$, keeping the sign-change half.
exercises.solution: At $1.5$, $f=1.375>0$, so retain $[1,1.5]$. At $1.25$, $f=-0.046875<0$, so retain $[1.25,1.5]$. This bracket has width $0.25$; its midpoint $1.375$ is within $0.125$ of the contained root.

exercises.question: Prove that $\sqrt{x}$ is right-continuous at the endpoint $0$ on $[0,1]$. For each $\varepsilon>0$, give a right-hand input bound that guarantees the output error is below $\varepsilon$.
exercises.hint: Use the one-sided epsilon definition at zero. What bound on $x$ makes $\sqrt{x}<\varepsilon$?
exercises.solution: The value is $\sqrt0=0$. As $x\to0^+$, $\sqrt x\to0$; explicitly, for $\varepsilon>0$, $0\le x<\varepsilon^2$ gives $|\sqrt x-0|<\varepsilon$. Thus the function is right-continuous at the endpoint $0$.

exercises.question: Prove $\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4$ with an explicit $\delta(\varepsilon)$.
exercises.hint: Bound $|x+2|$ after requiring $|x-2|<1$.
exercises.solution: If $|x-2|<1$, then $1<x<3$ and $|x+2|<5$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/5)$. Then $0<|x-2|<\delta$ gives $|x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|<5\delta\le\varepsilon$.

exercises.question: Prove $\lim_{x\to-1}x^2=1$ with an explicit $\delta(\varepsilon)$.
exercises.hint: Bound $|x-1|$ after requiring $|x+1|<1$.
exercises.solution: If $|x+1|<1$, then $-2<x<0$ and $|x-1|<3$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/3)$. For $0<|x+1|<\delta$, $|x^2-1|=|x+1||x-1|<3\delta\le\varepsilon$.

summary: Limits concern nearby inputs; continuity additionally requires agreement with the value at the point.
Limit laws and squeezing establish limits under explicit hypotheses; epsilon–delta proofs state the full tolerance guarantee.
Infinite limits describe unbounded outputs, whereas limits at infinity describe distant inputs.
Continuity on a closed interval guarantees intermediate values, providing the foundation for reliable root bracketing.
next: Chapter 5 applies limits to average rates over shrinking intervals, defining derivatives and explaining why continuity is necessary but insufficient for differentiability.
